summary:
Ausnox is an interactive Marswalk planning prototype. It helps people explore real planetary data through 2D maps and a Three.js 3D terrain view of part of Jezero Crater.

Using a USGS HiRISE-derived digital terrain model, Ausnox visualizes elevation and slope and calculates traversable outbound and return routes with A* pathfinding. Users can choose a hypothetical habitat, science destinations, and stops; compare route options; and estimate walking time, modeled daylight, and return margin using NASA Mars24-based calculations. NASA Mars Trek imagery and Perseverance rover-location references provide additional context.

The project makes complex Mars datasets easier to interpret while clearly separating observed data, derived calculations, and illustrative mission assumptions. Ausnox is an educational prototype, not operational astronaut navigation software.
details:
Ausnox — Navigating the Red Planet from Dawn to Dusk

What I Developed

Ausnox is an interactive Marswalk planning application developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge.

It transforms real planetary observations and scientific calculations into an accessible interface where users can explore Martian terrain, plan hypothetical surface excursions, and evaluate the effects of terrain and daylight on a proposed mission.

How Ausnox Works

Ausnox focuses on a verified area of Jezero Crater, near the Three Forks depot area and Skinner Ridge.

Interactive 2D and 3D Maps: Users can explore Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery and terrain using a traditional 2D map or a Three.js 3D terrain explorer. The 3D terrain geometry comes from the processed USGS HiRISE digital terrain model rather than artificially generated terrain.

Terrain and Route Analysis: The application uses elevation and derived slope information to calculate traversable routes using the A* pathfinding algorithm. Users can compare shortest-distance and lower-slope routes. The outbound and return routes are calculated independently.

Mission Planning: Users can establish a hypothetical habitat, select science destinations, add intermediate stops, and adjust illustrative mission assumptions such as walking speed, activity duration, and slope limits.

Martian Daylight: Ausnox implements solar-time calculations based on NASA's Mars24 algorithms to estimate geometric sunrise, sunset, and available daylight.

Mission Feasibility: The scientific engine combines route distance, walking time, science activities, daylight, and selected safety margins to assess whether a hypothetical Marswalk satisfies the chosen constraints.

Mission Simulation: An interactive timeline helps users understand the sequence of activities and remaining return margin during a simulated mission.

NASA Data and Resources

Ausnox integrates information associated with multiple NASA missions:

  • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter: HiRISE-derived terrain and HiRISE/CTX imagery.
  • Mars Global Surveyor: MOLA topographic imagery for regional context.
  • Mars 2020 Perseverance: Referenced rover locations used as science targets.
  • NASA GISS Mars24: Mathematical models for Martian timekeeping and daylight.

The underlying terrain data is processed from a USGS-published HiRISE digital terrain model. The application distinguishes measured observations from derived values and simulated assumptions.

Technologies Used

Ausnox was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Three.js, Zustand, and other open-source libraries.

Its scientific engine implements terrain-aware A* routing, coordinate transformations, Mars24-based calculations, and mission feasibility evaluation. Python-based geospatial processing was used to prepare and validate the terrain dataset.

The application is deployed through Vercel and operates directly in the browser.

Creativity and Intended Impact

Ausnox goes beyond displaying a static Martian map by connecting geographic exploration, terrain-aware route planning, and time-based mission constraints in one interactive experience.

Its goal is to make complex NASA planetary datasets easier to understand for students, space enthusiasts, and users who may not have advanced planetary-science backgrounds.

The project demonstrates how open scientific resources can support education and inspire new approaches to planetary exploration and mission-planning visualization.

Scientific Limitations

Ausnox is an educational prototype, not operational astronaut navigation software.

Terrain resolution cannot capture every surface hazard. Walking speeds, activity durations, and mission reserves are illustrative assumptions. The application does not provide real-time Mars weather or validated radiation-exposure forecasts.

A supplementary scientific validation test identified an unresolved possible registration difference of approximately 3 meters between the digital terrain model and some imagery. This limitation is documented and disclosed within the application.

AI-Assisted Development and Transparency

Generative AI tools, including OpenAI GPT models and Anthropic Claude Code, assisted with planning, software architecture, programming, UI/UX development, debugging, testing, and documentation.

AI-assisted implementations were integrated into the application and evaluated through automated tests and documented scientific validation procedures. The underlying NASA/USGS observational datasets were not presented as AI-generated observations.

Any AI-generated demonstration visuals or synthetic narration are disclosed separately in the accompanying media and metadata, where applicable.
